newsitem.title: CHINA: China investors hold cash after stock crackdown.
newsitem.headline: China investors hold cash after stock crackdown.

text.p: China has effectively chased speculative funds off its two bourses and many investors are now holding cash while they search for new opportunities to reap good returns, brokers and analysts said on Monday.

Market regulators in May stepped up a crackdown on stock speculation in Shanghai and Shenzhen after investor exuberance over the return of Hong Kong to China from British rule on July 1 pushed up prices by roughly 50 percent from early 1997.
"Share prices have definitely been brought down to a more suitable level," said a Shanghai Stock Exchange official, who declined to be named.

Beijing waded into the markets by boosting the new share issue quota for 1997, banning state enterprises and listed firms from speculative trading and barring state banks from share and state debt trading on the stock exchanges.
"In May and June, trading volume was very high," said an analyst at a European securities firm in Shanghai.

"These days volume has shrunk mainly because a lot of hot money from banks and state companies has been pushed out of the market," he said, adding that Shanghai's daily trading volume had slumped by more than half the levels of May and June.
The government's steps were largely aimed at the domestic currency A share market, but sentiment on the foreign currency B share market also took a hit, brokers said.
Although the government's execution of the cooling measures was clumsy at times, the moves would in the long run help the long-term development of the markets, they said.
"The crackdown helped season the regulators," said a broker at a foreign securities firm in Shanghai. "Next time around, they may be able to be more transparent in their actions."
Chinese investors currently had few choices on where to put their money and the stock market could again become a target of speculative funds, brokers said.
But retail investors were now content to hold cash and contemplate their next move, they said.

State banks had channelled some funds into a new interbank market for state debt spot and repo trading after their withdrawal from the two stock exchanges, but many were still sitting on the funds, analysts said.
"A lot of the speculative funds went back into cash, since there's no other place for it to go," said Bruce Richardson, chief representative for ABN AMRO Hoare Govett Group in Shanghai.
China's futures markets have been crippled by periodic crackdowns on speculation over the past three years, while the national foreign exchange market is also tightly regulated.
Some money was beginning to find its way into the secondary bond markets, where current yields of around 10 percent made them slightly more attractive than bank deposits, analysts said.
While such returns could not match those of China's stock markets, they were still quite attractive, said Qu Hongbin, chief economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Securities in Hong Kong.
"There are not many good investment opportunities in the real economy and business confidence is very low," Qu said.
Some of the funds could also flow into the booming Hong Kong stock market through unofficial and virtually undetectable channels, analysts said.
